title: Puerto Rico Medicaid Task Force Report 2027: Making the Case for the Obvious
description:
Another Report, the Same Emergency.

Roughly 40% of Puerto Rico relies on Medicaid, almost double the 21% average across the 50 states, and the program runs on a capped Section 1108 allotment instead of the open-ended federal match every state gets. The temporary fix from the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 lifted the island's matching rate from 55% to 76% and raised the ceiling to $3.825 billion by fiscal year 2027. When it expires, the match falls back to 55%, the ceiling drops to a 2019 baseline, and about $3.36 billion a year leaves the system. This episode reads the October 2026 report of the multi-sectoral Medicaid task force, the board that has to make the case for the obvious one more time: between 860,000 and 1 million people could lose coverage, and underfunding the island already costs federal taxpayers more than funding it would.

In this episode:

• An open tab versus a gift card. In the states, federal Medicaid money is open-ended: the government matches allowable costs with no cap, up to 83% for the poorest states. Puerto Rico gets a fixed allotment with a statutory base match of 55%. When the allotment runs out, every dollar after that is local. The 2023 boost let the island raise eligibility to 100% of the federal poverty level instead of a local, artificially low one, but expenditures for 2026 and 2027 are still projected to exceed even the higher cap.

• Fewer people, sicker people. The population fell almost 12% in a decade and the population under 18 fell nearly 38%, but 24.6% of residents are 65 or older against 18% in the states. Poverty is 40.5% against 12.5%; 60% to 70% of adults live with at least one chronic condition, hypertension runs 40% to 45%, and diabetes 17.8%. The healthy working-age taxpayers leave; the high-need patients stay. Of more than 81,000 people diagnosed with invasive cancer between 2019 and 2023, 42% relied on Medicaid in their first year of treatment.

• $74 a month. U.S. citizens in Puerto Rico are excluded by law from Supplemental Security Income. The island's substitute, Aid to the Aged, Blind and Disabled, is a capped grant Puerto Rico must match 25%, and it pays an average of about $74 a month. The same citizen on SSI in the states could receive up to $994.

• No long-term care, so the hospital is the long-term care. Medicaid funding limits mean no home- and community-based long-term services and supports: no personal care aides, no residential services for adults with intellectual disabilities. Family members quit their jobs to provide care, or the condition waits until it becomes an emergency. The island's only trauma hospital runs a -3.7% net margin; the average U.S. hospital earns +6.7%.

• The migration premium. In a 2023 Ipsos survey of adults who had recently moved to the mainland, 19% named health services among their top five reasons and 14% moved specifically to treat a health condition. Medicaid spending per enrollee was $3,293 in Puerto Rico in 2024 against $10,377 in the median state. The 15,303 Medicaid-eligible people who relocated that year cost the federal government an estimated $96.8 million on the mainland, against $41.8 million had they been covered at home: an extra $55 million in a single year, 2.3 times the price for the same citizens.

• The 2027 cliff. In fiscal year 2028 the island's uninsured rate would rise from 5.7% to roughly 30%, and the services added in 2024, home health, durable medical equipment, hospice and non-emergency transportation, would be the first at risk.

• Not a leaky bucket. Puerto Rico has met every CMS program integrity requirement. It launched an enterprise data warehouse in February 2026, verifies applicants' assets electronically with financial institutions, pays hospitals by diagnosis-related group instead of line item, and earns an extra $375 million a year from the same federal government for its compliance. It now pays physicians 100% of the Medicare Part B fee schedule to slow the brain drain.

The closing question: if capping Puerto Rico's Medicaid only moves the same citizens to states where their care costs the federal government two to three times as much, is the cap saving money, or just hiding the true cost of care on someone else's balance sheet?
